question: What is the primary purpose of disease surveillance in public health?

options.A: To punish healthcare workers who fail to report cases
options.B: The systematic collection, analysis, and interpretation of health data for action
options.C: To provide free medical treatment to all citizens in a region
options.D: To replace clinical nursing diagnoses with epidemiological research

explanation: Disease surveillance is defined as the systematic, ongoing collection, analysis, and interpretation of health-related data essential for planning and public health action. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: Why is disease surveillance particularly important for community health nurses in Nigeria?

options.A: It allows them to act as frontline observers to detect unusual disease patterns early
options.B: It exempts them from clinical bedside nursing duties
options.C: It guarantees automatic promotion within the ministry of health
options.D: It eliminates the need for any laboratory testing in rural clinics

explanation: Community health nurses serve as frontline observers who detect unusual disease patterns at the grassroots level, making surveillance vital for early response. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h1)

question: Which of the following is a primary objective of a public health surveillance system?

options.A: To rapidly detect epidemics and sudden outbreaks
options.B: To increase the cost of pharmaceutical drugs
options.D: To diagnose individual patients in tertiary care

explanation: A primary objective of surveillance is to detect epidemics and sudden outbreaks swiftly so that rapid containment measures can be implemented. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h2)

question: How do surveillance systems assist with health interventions over time?

options.A: By completely stopping all diseases permanently
options.B: By evaluating the impact of control and prevention programs
options.C: By reducing the salary of healthcare workers
options.D: By removing the need for community health education

explanation: Surveillance data are crucial for evaluating the impact of public health interventions and programs over time to ensure effective use of resources. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h2)

question: What characterizes passive disease surveillance?

options.A: Public health staff actively search door-to-door for sick patients
options.B: Healthcare providers routinely report cases to health authorities without active prompting
options.C: Data is only collected from a single high-tech national laboratory
options.D: Only laboratory-confirmed cases are ever recorded

explanation: Passive surveillance occurs when healthcare providers routinely report disease cases to health authorities on their own initiative as part of standard reporting duties. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the main advantage of syndromic surveillance during an emerging health threat?

options.A: It tracks pre-diagnostic symptoms for the earliest possible detection
options.B: It requires 100% laboratory confirmation before any report is made
options.C: It is cheaper and faster than passive surveillance in rural clinics
options.D: It completely eliminates the need for public health nurses

explanation: Syndromic surveillance tracks clinical signs and symptoms before formal laboratory diagnosis, enabling the earliest possible detection of threats. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h3)

question: What is the first core step in the public health surveillance process?

options.B: Data generation and collection at the frontline level
options.D: Evaluating the success of a vaccine campaign

explanation: The surveillance process begins with data generation and collection, where frontline health workers identify and record health events. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h4)

question: Why is data dissemination an essential part of the surveillance cycle?

options.A: It ensures that insights are shared with reporters, policymakers, and the community for action
options.B: It allows nurses to avoid clinical paperwork
options.C: It replaces the need for laboratory testing
options.D: It ensures all patient names are published publicly

explanation: Dissemination ensures that analyzed insights are returned to healthcare facilities, policymakers, and the community to guide timely and informed public health actions. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h4)

question: Which of the following is considered a non-traditional data source that can supplement disease surveillance?

options.B: School absenteeism logs and pharmacy sales records
options.D: World Health Organization global health treaties

explanation: Non-traditional sources like school absenteeism logs and pharmacy sales records can provide vital supplementary data, particularly in areas with limited formal healthcare access. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of using standardized case report forms in data collection?

options.A: To ensure consistency and accuracy of data across different clinics and regions
options.B: To increase the amount of paperwork required for nurses
options.C: To replace the need for patient interviews
options.D: To ensure that hospitals receive more financial funding

explanation: Standardized forms ensure consistency and accuracy across different facilities, which is essential for reliable surveillance data comparison. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h5)

question: How is a confirmed case typically distinguished from a suspected case?

options.A: A confirmed case has definitive laboratory-based proof of the pathogen
options.B: A suspected case is always more severe than a confirmed case
options.C: A confirmed case does not require any clinical symptoms
options.D: A suspected case can only be diagnosed by a national minister of health

explanation: A confirmed case requires definitive laboratory-based proof of the pathogen, whereas a suspected case is based primarily on compatible clinical symptoms. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h6)

question: What action is typically required for immediately reportable or notifiable diseases like cholera or yellow fever?

options.A: Waiting until the end of the year to compile an annual report
options.B: Urgent notification to local and national health authorities within 24 hours
options.C: Treating the patient at home without informing anyone
options.D: Destroying all clinic records related to the patient

explanation: Immediately reportable diseases require urgent notification within 24 hours to trigger rapid public health responses and containment. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h6)

question: What are the three fundamental epidemiological variables used when analyzing surveillance data?

options.B: Hospital budget, staff count, and drug supply
options.C: Patient weight, height, and blood type
options.D: Weather temperature, wind speed, and humidity

explanation: Data analysis evaluates health events across three core variables: time, place, and person, to identify patterns and anomalies. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h7)

question: What is the main goal of disseminating analyzed surveillance data to stakeholders?

options.A: To ensure that stakeholders have up-to-date intelligence to guide prevention and control actions
options.B: To increase the administrative workload of clinical nurses
options.C: To keep all health information strictly confidential from the public
options.D: To replace the need for physical patient examinations

explanation: Dissemination ensures that timely intelligence reaches health workers, policymakers, and communities to guide effective prevention and control actions. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h7)

question: How do community health nurses act as a bridge in disease surveillance?

options.A: By connecting grassroots households and community observations with the formal health system
options.B: By constructing bridges over rivers during rainy seasons
options.C: By acting as financial auditors for hospital budgets
options.D: By replacing national epidemiologists at ministries of health

explanation: Nurses act as a vital bridge by linking grassroots community observations and households with formal public health reporting and response structures. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h8)

question: Which of the following is a key responsibility of a community nurse during a disease outbreak?

options.A: Conducting contact tracing and educating the community on preventive practices
options.B: Closing down all local markets permanently
options.C: Manufacturing vaccines in the local clinic
options.D: Stopping all patient consultations to focus exclusively on paperwork

explanation: Community nurses play a key role in contact tracing, health education, specimen collection, and supporting outbreak containment efforts at the grassroots level. [learn more](GNS313_U4_T3#GNS313_U4_T3_h8)
